setupSteps: Read the placard and find the pin. The weight stack is a column of plates with a hole in each; a metal pin slides into the hole to pick the load. Put the pin in the lightest slot for your first set and push it fully in so it cannot slip. A beginner starting load from a reputable source: Not found.

Set the seat height first. Sit with your back flat on the pad and adjust the seat so the handles line up with mid-chest, about nipple height (NASM, ACE: handles no deeper than the front of the chest). Too low: the handles sit at shoulder level and the shoulders take more strain. Too high: the press angles upward and the shoulders take over (sources disagree on which is worse, but all agree on mid-chest).
Check your feet. Both feet flat on the floor, about hip-width apart (SparkPeople). If your feet do not reach, use the foot platform if the machine has one.
Back and shoulders. Hips back in the seat, shoulder blades pulled gently back and down against the pad (ACE: blades stay in contact with the backrest), chest up, ribs down.

Handle start position. If the machine has a start-position lever, use it so the handles begin where your elbows are about level with, or just behind, your chest line, not far behind. Some machines have an adjustable start-position arm; settings vary by brand. Ask staff if unsure.

Grip. Hold the handles with an even grip, wrists straight, over the middle of the palm. Neutral (palms facing each other) or overhand grips depend on the handles; use the one that feels comfortable on the wrists.
Test a very light rep before loading more.
Check the plate pegs and sleeves. Load equal plates on both sides if the machine is a two-arm type, and push them fully on to the pegs. Add a clip or collar if the machine has one.

Start light. Begin with the lightest plates; many plate-loaded machines have a built-in lever ratio so the same plates feel lighter or heavier than on a bar. The exact load is Not found; judge it by reps in reserve (section 7).
Release the safety catch (a stopper or a foot lever) before the first rep, and lock it again at the end.
Converging handles: the arms travel inward as you press and may allow your hands to come closer together at the top; keep the elbows slightly in front of the shoulder line the whole way.
Fixed (parallel or diverging) handles: the path stays on a line; set the seat very carefully because it has less margin for error.

steps.title: Sit and lock in
steps.action: Sit with your back flat on the pad, feet flat, hands on the handles at mid-chest.
steps.feel: Back and hips supported; chest lightly open.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear over shoulder, back on the pad, handle at mid-chest, forearms roughly pointing forward. Front: shoulders level, elbows slightly below the handles.

steps.title: Set the shoulder blades
steps.action: Pull your shoulder blades gently back and down against the pad.
steps.feel: Chest slightly lifted; front of shoulders not rolled forward.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders back against the pad, not rounded. Front: no shrug.

steps.title: Brace
steps.action: Tighten your stomach lightly, keep your head resting back or neutral, and plant your feet.
steps.breathing: Hold a small breath for a moment only; do not hold it through the rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: lower back stays in contact with the pad; no lifting of the hips.

steps.title: Press out
steps.action: Push the handles forward until your arms are almost straight.
steps.feel: Chest and front shoulders working, triceps finishing the push.
steps.visualCheck: Side: handles travel in a smooth line at chest height; shoulders stay down and back. Front: elbows stay in front of the chest, about 45-75 degrees from the torso (est.).

steps.title: Stop before locking
steps.action: Finish with elbows straight but not snapped (ACE: straight, not locked).
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle near 160-175 degrees (est.), shoulders not shrugged up.

steps.title: Return under control
steps.action: Let the handles come back slowly until the elbows are about at chest level (upper arms roughly in line with the torso).
steps.feel: Chest lengthening under load; no sharp pinch at the front of the shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: Side: handles stop at mid-chest; weight stack plates do not clang at the bottom.

steps.title: Repeat smoothly for the planned reps, keeping the shoulder blades on the pad
Finish the set. After the last rep, re-engage the safety catch or release the stack with the foot lever, let the handles rest, and stand up once they are still
steps.visualCheck: Side: stack down, handles at rest, then you stand.

commonMistakes.title: Seat too low or too high
commonMistakes.text: Seat too low or too high. Why: the handles sit at shoulder level or above the chest, which can strain the front of the shoulder and the rotator cuff (retailer and trainer sources; NASM says mid-chest). Fix: handles at mid-chest, nipple height.

commonMistakes.title: Shoulders rolling forward and shrugging
commonMistakes.text: Shoulders rolling forward and shrugging. Why: the front of the shoulder takes the load and the chest stops working. Fix: blades back and down on the pad, lighter weight until the chest stays open.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flared to 90 degrees
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flared to 90 degrees. Why: modelled shoulder-joint loads are higher in some flared patterns (Noteboom 2024 is a model, not an injury study), and coaches say it reduces chest work. Fix: elbows 45-75 degrees from the body (est.).

commonMistakes.title: Locking the elbows hard at the top
commonMistakes.text: Locking the elbows hard at the top. Why: loads the joint, not the muscle (ACE: straight but not locked). Fix: stop just short of straight.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the hips or arching the back to push
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the hips or arching the back to push. Why: the load is too heavy and the lower back takes over. Fix: lower the weight, keep the back on the pad.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the handles slam back
commonMistakes.text: Letting the handles slam back. Why: loud, jolts the shoulders, and wastes the lowering phase. Fix: 2-3 seconds down and stop before the stack touches.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath on every rep
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath on every rep. Why: raises blood pressure (see Safety). Fix: breathe out as you press.

commonMistakes.title: Using the machine like a fixed "easy" exercise and pushing to failure with no spotter
commonMistakes.text: Using the machine like a fixed "easy" exercise and pushing to failure with no spotter. Why: a plate-loaded machine without a safety catch can trap you. Fix: set the safety stopper, finish with 2-3 reps in reserve.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems (impingement, rotator cuff, past dislocation): a seat set too low or the handles too far back puts the shoulder in a stressed position. Use a smaller range, a lighter load, a neutral grip if available, and stop if you feel a pinch in the front of the shoulder (see the table).
Lower back pain: the back pad supports the spine, so the machine is usually easier than free weights. Keep the back on the pad and do not arch to press.
High blood pressure: breath-holding (Valsalva) raises blood pressure. Breathe out on the press and avoid sets to failure.
Chest, rib or breastbone injury, or recent chest surgery (including pacemaker implants): the pressing range can aggravate healing tissue. Only with approval.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis: see the table.
